To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) acoustic models derived from major languages can be used to build LVCSR systems for under-resourced languages without any transcribed acoustic training data, and (ii) the new system is a powerful tool for accelerating resource production in the under-resourced language.

the best results for the target language are obtained by combining the acoustic models of two of the three source languages (French and German) and that the best results are obtained when using a multilingual acoustic model for each of the two source languages.

(i) multilingual acoustic models can be built for under-resourced languages without any transcribed data, and (ii) the resulting ASR system can be used for automatic transcriptions that can then be used to bootstrap the resource development for such languages.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether a first LVCSR system can be built for Luxembourgish without the use of any transcribed Luxembourgish training data.
the development of a first large vocabulary ASR for a language with a very small amount of transcribed audio training material.
the development of ASR systems for under-resourced languages.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
multilingual acoustic modelling is not a viable option for Luxembourgish, and that the language is not a Germanic one.
the system is able to transcribe Luxembourgish speech with reasonable accuracy.
the multilingual acoustic model outperforms all the others.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have built an ASR system for Luxembourgish, a language that is not spoken in the US, UK or Canada, and that is not spoken by more than 300.000 speakers.

the system is able to transcribe Luxembourgish speech with 10% absolute error reduction compared to the baseline, which is an error reduction of 50% relative to a baseline system without acoustic models.

the system we developed can be used to accelerate the production of a large vocabulary ASR for Luxembourgish, which in turn can be used to bootstrap the creation of a Luxembourgish speech corpus, a first for Luxembourgish, and thus to accelerate further the production of a Luxembourgish LVCSR system.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the use of multilingual acoustic models for ASR is feasible even when there is no labelled training data for the target language, and that the use of such multilingual models is beneficial even when there is a large amount of transcribed audio training for the target language.

the use of a large multilingual acoustic model trained with a large number of languages can be used to bootstrap the acoustic modelling of a new language, even in the absence of any labelled acoustic training data for that language.
the multilingual approach is a promising way to build ASR systems for languages with limited training resources.
